case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

1. Mental Demand

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. ## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.
